headline: John Ternus becomes Apple's chief executive as Tim Cook moves to executive chairman
dek: The handover takes effect on 1 September, the date Apple set when it announced the succession in April. Cook led the company for fifteen years.
summary: Apple's hardware engineering chief John Ternus takes over as chief executive on 1 September, with Tim Cook becoming executive chairman after fifteen years in the role.

image.alt: An empty meeting room with a long table and chairs beside a window in a modern office building

body.text: John Ternus becomes chief executive of Apple on 1 September, taking over from Tim Cook, who has held the job since August 2011. Cook becomes executive chairman of the company's board. The date was fixed more than four months ago: Apple set it out in a newsroom release on 20 April, which said the change would take effect on 1 September 2026.

Two publications that cover the company closely, *9to5Mac* and *MacRumors*, both reported on 31 August that it was Cook's final day as chief executive and that Ternus would take the title the following day. Neither reported any change to the timetable Apple published in April, and no fresh statement from the company was found in the material read for this article.

Apple's April release describes Ternus, then senior vice president of hardware engineering, as the next chief executive, and says Cook will become executive chairman of the board. It gives one description of what that role involves: assisting with certain aspects of the company, including engaging with policymakers around the world. The release does not set out the position's duties in any further detail, and no fuller description was found.
The same release records a second board change. Arthur Levinson, who had been non-executive chairman, becomes lead independent director.
John Ternus has the mind of an engineer, the soul of an innovator, and the heart to lead with integrity and with honor.
body.cite: Tim Cook, chief executive of Apple, in the company's 20 April newsroom release

body.text: Ternus is quoted in the same release saying he is grateful for the opportunity. Levinson, in his own quoted remark, describes Cook's leadership as having transformed the company. All three quotations come from Apple's own announcement rather than from an interview, and each is the company's account of its own transition.
I am profoundly grateful for this opportunity to carry Apple's mission forward.
body.cite: John Ternus, then senior vice president of hardware engineering, in Apple's 20 April newsroom release

body.text: Apple's release gives Ternus's career inside the company in outline. He joined in 2001, on the product design team; became vice president of hardware engineering in 2013; and joined the executive team in 2021. Before Apple he worked as a mechanical engineer at Virtual Research Systems. He holds a bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Pennsylvania. *MacRumors* described him on 31 August as the company's hardware engineering chief and put his time at Apple at twenty-five years.

That is a narrower public record than a chief executive of a company this size usually arrives with. Ternus has spent his working life on hardware rather than in a general management or finance role, and he has not run a public company before. Whether that matters is not something the reporting read for this article settles, and it is not a question anyone can answer from a start date.

*9to5Mac* reported that Ternus is expected to lead Apple's presentation at an event on 9 September, and listed products the company is expected to show there. Those are expectations reported by the outlet, not commitments Apple has made in anything read here. The same article relayed a Bloomberg report that Cook's attention as executive chairman will fall on relationships with the United States government and with China, and described that report as unconfirmed. Bloomberg's own account was not read for this article, and Apple's April release says only that the role involves engaging with policymakers.

There is also no public account, in the sources read, of what else changes inside the company on 1 September — whether other senior roles move, or whether the executive team Apple listed in April stays as it is. A leadership change announced four months in advance and executed on schedule is, on the evidence available today, exactly that: a scheduled handover that happened on the day it was set for.

body.title: How this story was sourced
items: Apple's own 20 April newsroom release, for the terms of the transition and every quotation
Two independent outlets that cover Apple, 9to5Mac and MacRumors, both published on 31 August
No market figures are reported here: the financial coverage found either carried no named authority for its numbers or was analyst commentary rather than fact

uncertain: Apple issued no statement on 31 August or 1 September that was found in this research; the day's coverage rests on the company's April announcement.
The duties of the executive chairman role beyond the single phrase in Apple's April release — engaging with policymakers around the world — are not publicly described.
That Ternus will lead the 9 September event, and what Apple will show there, are expectations reported by 9to5Mac rather than announcements by the company.
The Bloomberg report on Cook's focus as executive chairman was relayed by 9to5Mac and described there as unconfirmed. Bloomberg's own article was not read.
Whether any other senior leadership or board changes take effect alongside the handover could not be established.
The quotations here are taken from Apple's own release. MacRumors carried the Cook quotation in a shorter form; the primary release's wording is used because it is the source of the statement.
No independent assessment of the transition — from a shareholder, a director, or an outside analyst speaking on the record — was found in the sources read.
